title: Phosphorus-Mediated Reductive C--N Bond Coupling: A Path to Functionalized Azaheterocycles
abstract: Nitrogen heterocycles are of significant industrial interest due to their abundance in natural products and other organic molecules with great biological potential. As such, methods which can readily access C – N bonds are of great synthetic interest. Current prevailing strategies, such as the Ullman, Buchwald-Hartwig, and Chan-Lam coupling reactions, are transition-metal dominated, requiring the usage of either copper or noble metals. Researchers in the Radosevich group have previously synthesized a biphilic phosphetane catalyst which catalyzes bond formation between nitroarenes and phenylboronic acids. This new coupling strategy is fundamentally different from previous palladium-based methods in that it operates via a P III /P V =O redox cycle. While this phosphetane catalyst is easily synthesized and can be used at reasonable loadings (15%), its major drawback is that it is not commercially available. Phosphines, as O-atom acceptors, were of special interest as alternative reagents, although their nucleophilic nature ensures that they cannot be regenerated. In my research, we showed that stoichiometric amounts of triethylphosphine, an inexpensive commercial agent, can drive the deoxygenative coupling of nitroarenes and boronic acids to generate di(hetero)arylamine products in a direct synthetic operation without the need for any transition metal additives. A variety of diarylamine products were prepared in good yield using this method, revealing versatility with regards to functional groups on both coupling partners. Additionally, this method offers access to traditionally difficult substrates such as nitroarenes containing electron-withdrawing groups. These C--N coupling techniques can then be used to access difficult azaheterocyclic frameworks with multiple sites for reaction. If one were to add groups to a benzimidazole, the presence of two nitrogen atoms which can tautomerize ensures two possible sites for addition. When the molecule is symmetric—as is the parent nucleus—this is not a problem, but in asymmetric instances, it is nontrivial to ensure functional groups end up on the correct side of the molecule. Here, we use the phosphetane catalyst described earlier, which can also catalyze an intramolecular Cadogan cyclization, to synthesize various azaheterocycles. This method allows us to approach pharmaceutically relevant molecules, and has been successfully applied to the synthesis of oxindoles, indoles, quinoxalines, and benzimidazoles.

title: Oxidative Coupling of Methane Using Mn-Na 2 WO 4 /TiO 2 Catalysts: effect of the Support on Reaction Performance
abstract: Ethylene is a vital chemical for the synthesis of most petrochemical products, and highly demanded in the industrial field. As the demand increases, various methods of converting abundant methane into useful ethylene are drawing more attention. The current commercial process of producing ethylene from methane is a two-stage process that first converts methane into syngas (steam reforming) and then synthesizes it with ethylene. However, this process suffers from low energy efficiency and high capital and operating costs. The OCM is energetically more efficient than endothermic steam reforming because it is exothermic, and this one-step process can reduce capital and operating costs. However, the OCM can proceed to deep oxidation and homogeneous reaction to form CO or CO 2 . Thus, avoiding formation of CO or CO 2 is critical for improving yield of C 2 products. The Mn- Na 2 WO 4 /SiO 2 catalyst has shown promise for OCM. In this study, the Mn-Na 2 WO 4 was supported with various types of TiO 2 (Mn-Na 2 WO 4 /TiO 2 ) to determine the most promising catalyst to enhance C 2 yield and methane conversion. These catalysts were also further compared to a previously studied Mn- Na 2 WO 4 /SiO 2 catalyst. Each catalyst was prepared using incipient wetness impregnation method followed by a specific calcination procedure. The tests were conducted over a range of temperatures from 725 to 800 o C in a fixed-bed reactor. The gases exiting from the reactor were analyzed using a gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector. The surface area and crystallinity of catalysts were analyzed using BET method and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. In this study, the best catalyst was determined to be 1.9% Mn – 5% Na 2 WO 4 /TiO 2 (A), which has the largest surface area among the examined TiO 2 supports, suggesting that an increased surface area of the supporting metal may result in enhanced C 2 selectivity and methane conversion. In this context, future investigations are necessary to understand relationship or correlation between catalyst performance and surface area of the supporting catalysts.

title: The Synthesis and Reaction Kinetics of Reversible Epoxies in a Diels Alder Reaction
abstract: Epoxies are an important class of thermosetting polymers for many long-term applications such as adhesives, structural materials, paints, and coatings. Due to their thermosetting nature, epoxies are hard and robust, unfortunately they also are hard to remove, recycle and reuse. Epoxies capable of reverse polymerization are being studied in order to address these issues. In this research, reversible epoxies were synthesized by introducing the Diels-Alder reaction groups to epoxy monomers. A Diels-Alder cycloadduct was formed from the reaction of 1,1'-(Methylenedi-4,1-phenylene) bismaleimide and furfuryl glycidyl ether. Formation of the Diels-Alder cycloadduct was confirmed using Fourier Transform-Infrared (FTIR) Spectrometry. Next, the forward and reverse Diels-Alder reaction – corresponding to re-polymerization and depolymerization, respectively – was monitored by FTIR measurements at 90 oC and 110 oC as a function of exposure time. FT-IR measurements were taken for the sample at various temperatures from 90-120°C. FT-IR absorption peaks relevant to the reverse Diels-Alder reaction were gradually stronger as longer exposure time at 90 oC and 110 oC. The equilibrium shift was observed toward the reverse reaction dominant side at higher temperature by comparison of FTIR spectra at 90 oC and 110 oC. The reversible epoxy resins will be cured with various curing agents and their reaction kinetics will be studied.

title: TiO 2 Catalysts: Micropowders and Nanofibers in Sustainable Reactions
abstract: TiO 2 Catalysts: Micropowders and Nanofibers in Sustainable Reactions A. Jernigan 1 , S. Nealy 2 , W. Maniukiewicz 3 , M. Modelska 3 , M. Binczarski 3 , T. Maniecki 3 , I. Witonska 3 , and A. Stanishevsky 2 , C. West 1 1 Department of Chemical Engineering, University of South Alabama, USA 2 Department of Physics, University of Alabama at Birmingham, USA 3 Institute of General and Ecological Chemistry, Faculty of Chemistry, Łódź University of Technology, Poland Catalytic technologies are vital in the advancement and development of many industries, including chemical, biological, and environmental. One area of focus in catalysis for several decades has been trying to find an efficient means of generating clean hydrogen, as this remains a barrier to widespread implementation of environmentally friendly hydrogen fuel cell technologies. An abundant source of hydrogen is water but liberating hydrogen from water is limited by both reaction kinetics and thermodynamics. Using photocatalysis with readily available biofuels as sacrificial reagents addresses those issues in part and presents the opportunity to harness solar energy to drive the reaction. The most studied photocatalyst is titania, and this work investigates the potential of titania nanofibers for those applications. Some of the inherent disadvantages are addressed using small amounts of other metals, such as its relative inactivity in the visible light range and rapid reversal of electron excitation. One metal incorporated is platinum, which is known to improve hydrogen generation rates, but other, less expensive metals are to be to reduce the amount of platinum needed and thus reduce the catalyst cost. In catalyst optimization, there is always a focus on finding ways to increase the available surface area and thus the efficiency and rate of reaction. Amid this push for smaller technologies, attention has been recently drawn to the potential of nanomaterials as an alternative to micromaterials in catalysis. Nanofibers are gaining significant interest as an alternative to micropowders with the advantage of greatly increased active surface area without the issue of agglomeration as is seen in nanopowders. In this work, TiO 2 nanofibers synthesized using needleless AC electrospinning were prepared for comparison to TiO 2 micropowders through the screening reaction of photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 to produce methanol. Future plans are to compare the sustainable production of hydrogen by photoreforming of ethanol on TiO2 nanofibers and micropowders doped with CuO and Pt. title: Catalytic Methane Dehydroaromatization with Microwave Heating
abstract: In industry, methane is converted into aromatics through an indirect route: methane to syn-gas and then syn-gas to aromatics. Methane dehydroaromatization (DHA) is a direct route that would be more economical. The DHA process we use is a catalytic reaction involving a zeolite, a microporous aluminosilicate mineral, for higher selectivity of desired aromatics. Due to the thermodynamic unfavorability of the reaction, high temperature operating conditions are required. At high temperatures, coking (solid carbon depositions) of the catalyst occurs and inhibits the reaction. Microwave (MW) heating of the catalyst is currently under investigation. The main advantage is selective heating which can reduce coking. By incorporating metals such as gallium, into the structure, the hypothesis is that the metals induce dipoles which can increase MW sensitivity. Current work involves synthesis of zeolites with different metal compositions and silicon to aluminum ratios in the framework to study how MW sensitivity is affected.

title: Synthesis of an Alloy-Based Ni-Fe/C Catalyst for the Alkaline Oxygen Evolution Reaction
abstract: Hydrogen gas is industrially relevant as a raw material for numerous chemical processes, including high-volume industrial chemicals such as ammonia and methanol. Currently, hydrogen is produced using reforming processes that involve fossil fuels and result in large releases of pollutants like CO 2 . Hydrogen production using electrolysis is a benign alternative. Alkaline anion-exchange membrane electrolyzers are promising for clean hydrogen production because the noncorrosive environment of the alkaline electrolyte enables the use of non-precious metal catalysts. However, practical implementation of these electrolyzers is hindered by high overpotentials for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). The oxidizing conditions of OER also affect the stability and conductivity of catalysts, leading to poor performance. Ni-based catalysts are widely studied for OER in alkaline conditions; furthermore, incorporation of Fe into Ni catalysts has shown promise by decreasing the onset potential compared to pure Ni. We are studying Ni–Fe composites derived from homogeneous metallic alloy precursors with the goal of creating alkaline OER catalysts that exhibit improved electron transport properties than those derived from pure oxides. We synthesized Ni–Fe alloy nanoparticles on an oxidized Vulcan carbon support using a wet-impregnation technique. The as-synthesized catalyst was activated for OER using electrochemical cycling. Systematic variation of carbon and Fe content in the Ni–Fe/C catalysts showed that a catalyst with 70:30 ratio of Ni:Fe and 48 wt% carbon content gave the smallest onset overpotential of ~270 mV. This catalyst attained 10 mA/cm 2 at an overpotential of 300 mV in 0.1 M KOH. It also exhibited enhanced activity at higher electrolyte concentration and at elevated temperature, but its stability was poor in concentrated electrolyte. Work is now focused on understanding the origin of this stability limitation.

title: Solar Water Disinfection Using Visible Light
abstract: Abstract: Stable In Situ H 2 O 2 Generation from an Au nanoparticle/SnO 2 System Author: Sarah Glass Metal/Semiconductor heterojunctions are an attractive solution for photodisinfection of water. These systems use sunlight to oxidize water and reduce dissolved O 2 to form reactive oxygen species (ROS) which can kill bacteria and viruses in water. Commonly used semiconductors for these systems are TiO 2 and ZnO both of which utilize only the ultraviolet (UV) portion of sunlight (~5% of the spectrum by energy). This is due to the bandgap of these semiconductors being greater than 3 eV. If the visible portion of sunlight was able to be used, a more effective system could be made. Visible active semiconductors like C 3 N 4 have been widely pursued but suffer from instability in aqueous media. An alternative approach is to use metal nanoparticles to drive plasmonic and interband transitions to generate “hot” carriers (e.g. holes and electrons) that are separated at the metal/semiconductor junction. Gold nanoparticles are ultrastrong absorbers of visible light, which makes up 40% of the solar spectrum. This opens the opportunity for a more efficient system that uses ~8x more light provided by the sun. Here we present the Au-nanoparticle/SnO 2 system that uses a wide-bandgap semiconductor, Tin Oxide, and plasmon resonance effects from gold nanoparticles. Gold nanoparticles strongly absorb visible light through their plasmon resonances and interband transitions with an absorption spectrum that is highly tunable based on the size and shape of the particle and the local environment they are in. SnO 2 is a highly stable, wide bandgap semiconductor that does not absorb visible light due to its wide bandgap (e.g. > 3.8 eV). It also has a favorable conduction band alignment with gold accepting the hot-electron and driving O 2 reduction at the SnO 2 /water interface. Our Au nanoparticle/SnO 2 systems results show that visible light can be used to generate H 2 O 2 . The test results support our initial hypothesis that using a stable wide bandgap semiconductor in conjunction with metal nanoparticles will generate ROS using visible light (> 450 nm).

title: Learning on the Job: An Active Learning Calculator for Atomistic Simulations
abstract: Neural network potentials have been used to accurately predict the energy and forces on atomic structures, acting as suitable substitutes for traditional electronic structure calculators. However, these predictions often diverge from true values when the neural network encounters images that deviate considerably from those found in the training set. In these cases, it would be desirable to include this image in the training set and re-train the network so it can better understand this region of the potential energy surface, but the manual selection of these images can be tedious and impractical. We present a method whereby a bootstrap ensemble of neural network calculators is used as a hands-free calculator that can identify poorly understood regions on the potential energy surface and retrain the calculator as necessary: for every image, an assessment of prediction certainty is made by evaluating the ensemble width, used as a measure for uncertainty. For images where the ensemble is uncertain, we call the electronic structure calculator and retrain the ensemble calculator on that image. A scheme for accelerated retraining of the neural network is also presented within. We apply this calculator to a 400-image sample of a single water molecule where one of the bond lengths and the bond angle is varied. We show the ability for the ensemble calculator to train itself when it is uncertain about an image, and display how retraining on just a few images allows the calculator to understand the region much better. This active learning calculator should allow for the hands-free training of accurate neural networks to perform electronic structure calculations through sample regions not covered by the training data, considerably reducing computation time and cost for future calculations that retread previously investigated sections of the potential energy surface.

title: Synthesis of Molybdenum Trioxide and Characteristics of H x MoO 3 Bronze Formation
abstract: Many modern chemical processes rely on highly polluting petroleum as a hydrogen source. Replacing petroleum with a cleaner alternative, such as water, could greatly enhance the sustainability of the chemical industry. Electrochemical methods allow the conversion of water into hydrogen; however, there is currently not a good understanding of how to integrate such electrochemical techniques into existing industrial reactions. With the goal of improving the sustainability of industrial chemical conversions, the gap between thermal and electrochemical catalysis needs to be bridged. Reducible metal oxides, such as tungsten trioxide (WO 3 ) and molybdenum trioxide (MoO 3 ), are useful models for these studies, as they can take up hydrogen both thermally (hydrogen spillover) and electrochemically (hydrogen intercalation). Our group recently reported on these processes in WO 3 , 1 but MoO 3 is known to have a higher hydrogen capacity. 2 This suggests that MoO 3 might exhibit enhanced reactivity, and so this work focuses on hydrogen uptake in MoO 3 . Two MoO 3 synthesis methods were investigated in order to produce a stable, reducible oxide. The selected method produced MoO 3 with an orthorhombic crystal structure, confirmed using XRD. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed to probe intercalation dynamics, where multiple discrete intercalation events were observed. Comparison to CVs of WO 3 reveal the MoO 3 has a lower overpotential for intercalation suggesting hydrogen insertion into MoO 3 is faster than into WO 3 . This study provides a foundation for further work on hydrogen uptake in H x MoO 3 and provides evidence that MoO 3 might be more useful than WO 3 for thermo-electrochemical hydrogenation chemistries. title: Novel Energy Transfer Mechanism for Dielectric Cu 2 o Nanostructures in Photocatalysis.
abstract: Most Plasmonic Metal Nanocatalysts (PMN) are plagued by inherent joule loss, band-gap limitations and the inability to showcase strong magnetic fields. In addition, several of the metal catalysts currently being used in industrial and pharmaceutical applications are toxic in nature and require expensive downstream operations. Fortunately, in the past few years, copper-based photocatalysts have been identified as an alternative to conventional catalysts. These copper-based catalysts are appealing due to their relative abundance, low cost, low toxicity and heterogenous nature. Previous reports suggest that researchers believe copper-based photocatalysts undergo energy transfers via plasmonic mechanisms as a result of Localized Surface Plasmon Resonance effects (LSPR) and standard semiconductor mechanisms that come into play once the semiconductor material’s bandgap energy barrier is exceeded. A new energy transfer theory was developed. Through novel experimental modeling and computational methods (FDTD simulations), mechanism types were isolated and then tested for degradation under various conditions. The concept demonstrated in our study unveils a new way to conduct solar light harvesting and photocatalysis. Although we demonstrated the concept using Cu 2 O particles, this concept can be broadly applied to other metal oxide semiconductor particles including titanium dioxide. The successful degradations narrowed down the mechanism possibilities and provided statistical support for this theory in application in not only photocatalysis, but an abundance of industries such as but not limited to: pharmaceutical, energy fuels, thin film solar cells, CO 2 reduction, specialty chemicals, agrochemicals, as well as water decontamination among other related industries.

title: Raman-Spectrokinetics for Gaining Insights on Support Effects of Supported Vanadium Oxide Catalysts
abstract: Understanding the link between observed structure and measured reactivity of supported metal oxide catalysts remains a challenging goal for the complex catalytic systems used in oxidative and non-oxidative dehydrogenation of light hydrocarbons. [1] Supported ternary metal oxide catalysts are one such system; their reactivity is influenced by catalyst coverage, relative amounts of species on the support, and the properties the of support. In the study presented, we used a combination of operando Raman spectroscopy and conventional time-resolved reaction kinetics to determine experimentally the redox reaction rates of surface species directly from the Raman spectra. This approach, coined Raman-spectrokinetic, overcomes a major limitation associated with elucidating kinetic parameters by conventional methods, via mass spectrometry (MS) and gas chromatography (GC). The Raman-spectrokinetic approach allows for observation of reaction rates at a specific catalytic site whereas conventional MS and GC analyses only provide the sample’s overall reaction rates (average rates from the entire samples’ sites). The study presented is a continuation of an earlier study which explored the oxidation of (VO x ) m /(NbO y ) n /SiO 2 catalysts. [2] Herein, we aim to elaborate on earlier work by reporting on the effects of catalyst support material by utilizing the Raman-spectrokinetic approach to gain new insights on the oxidation kinetics of supported vanadium oxide catalysts, following the evolution/depletion of the vandyl (V=O) vibration as a function of O 2 /H 2 concentration. With the knowledge that turnover frequency in catalysts remains constant as a function of coverage, our observation of the same phenomena via Raman-spectrokinetics renders support for the validity of the method. The goal of this study was to broaden our use of the Raman-spectrokinetic approach into reactivity of metal oxides at different MO x coverage (2D and 3D species), on different supports (SiO 2 , Al 2 O 3 , TiO 2 , ZrO 2 ), and with different surface structures. The insights gained in investigating the effects of these variables on reactivity and stability will further ongoing efforts to rationally design catalysts and achieve unprecedented catalytic performance with supported metal oxide catalysts. title: Nickel Oxide Silica Based and Commercial Nickel Oxide Nanosorbcats for Adsorption of Cationic and Anionic Dyes Followed By Thermo-Oxidative Decomposition
abstract: Wastewater contains a variety of pollutants that are basically classified into organic such as dyes and inorganic substances. The contamination of surface and groundwater with synthetic dyes is a serious environmental problem and is a threat to human beings. These dyes could be cationic, anionic, or neutral. For instance, many industries use pigments to color their products such as textiles, plastics, paper, and so forth. The discharge of the produced wastewater effluents into the environment is worrying for toxicological and aesthetical reasons. Therefore, their removal from wastewater is of great interest. All processes for removing such pollutants from wastewater have their own limitations. However, the adsorption process is recognized to be an effective and economic process for cleaning wastewater. In addition, adsorptive remediation of wastewater on metal-oxide-based nanoparticles has been reported in the literature extensively. Recent studies showed significant awareness of metal oxides as nanoadsorbents and nanocatalysts (nanosorbcats) for cleaning wastewater, due to their individual chemical and physical properties, which make them ascendant to the conventional adsorbent/catalysts. Herein, in this study, the employment of in-house prepared nickel oxide silica-based (SBN)s and commercial nickel oxide (NiO) nanoparticles as nanosorbcats for cleaning up synthetic wastewater was investigated. Different model molecule pollutants; mainly methylene blue (MB) and bromocresol green (BCG) exemplifying cationic and anionic pollutants, respectively, were removed from synthetic wastewater samples by SBNs and NiO nanoparticles. Batch isotherm adsorption studies in addition to kinetics and thermodynamics were performed for the removal of both dyes from wastewater. The experimental adsorption data has been modeled using the Sips adsorption isotherm model to understand the adsorption behavior of these molecules. Fast adsorption kinetics of both nanoparticles have been observed; NiO nanoparticles took 60 minutes to reach saturation of BCG while SBNs took only 2 minutes for the case of MB. Moreover, both nanoparticles have shown high uptakes of about 99% and 96% at low concentrations of MB and BCG. Furthermore, thermodynamic parameters like the changes in free Gibbs energy (ΔG), enthalpy (ΔH), and entropy (ΔS) of the system were calculated. The catalytic activity behavior of spent nanoparticles was investigated via thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA), to check out the applicability of the nanosorbcats concept. Consequently, the regeneration, uptake saturation capacities and the performances of spent SBNs and commercial NiO nanoparticles after each adsorption cycle were studied and compared with the virgin ones. The detailed findings of this study will be discussed further during the poster presentation.

title: Metal Containing ZSM-5 Catalysts for the Dry Reforming of Methane: Exploring Synergistic Effects
abstract: The abundance of natural gas in the U.S. brought by the development of new fracking technologies for its extraction has triggered a notable renaissance of the U.S. chemical manufacturing industry. The selective activation of C-H bonds in the most abundant component in natural gas, methane, is one of the greatest challenges in catalysis. Methane can be converted into raw materials or commodity chemicals as follow: i) indirectly via syngas or ii) directly via, for instance, selective oxidation or dehydroaromatization. Along with methane, emphasis has been placed on the utilization of CO 2 to produce chemicals and fuels do to their abundance and negative impact to the environment. Both CH 4 and CO 2 are the main contributors of the greenhouse effect. As a result, Dry Reforming of Methane (DRM) is an attractive route to convert CH 4 and CO 2 into syngas with an H 2 /CO ratio of 1:1, which is the optimal ratio to produce liquid hydrocarbons through the Fischer-Tropsch process. However, among other factors, the multiple undesired side reactions such as methane thermal degradation, carbon monoxide disproportionation, and water gas shift has, have limited the potential application of DRM at an industrial scale. These reactions adversely affect the H 2 /CO ratio and the overall catalyst’s performance. The major challenge to address, as a result of the mentioned side-reactions, is the rapid catalyst deactivation due to the formation of coke. In this study, we aim to improve DRM using a series of Fe/Ni/ZSM-5 catalysts. First, various methodologies have been used to prepare these materials trying to determine the most important variables influencing the final bulk and surface structure of the catalyst. We use various characterization techniques such as N 2 -physisorption, X-Ray diffraction (XRD), X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and Raman spectroscopy. Reactivity tests are performed in a home-made reaction setup equipped with various mass flow controllers, a stainless-steel reactor, a tubular furnace with a temperature controller, and a gas chromatograph (GC) for the analysis of the products. Steady-state kinetics has shown a stable catalytic activity and selectivity towards syngas for Fe/Ni/ZSM-5 compared to the Ni/ZSM-5 catalyst, indicating that Fe is suppressing the formation of coke during the reaction. We aim to determine the variables and the optimal catalyst composition to enhance the catalytic performance of conventional Ni-based catalysts. We will also perform in-situ/opernaro Raman studies to compliment the kinetic data and stablish a more conclusive structure-reactivity/selectivity/stability relationship.

title: Role of Confinement, Molecular Connectivity and Flexibility on Entropic Driven Surface Segregation of Polymer-Colloid Mixtures
abstract: Relative surface affinity between polymers and colloids are leveraged in many applications like filtration, adhesion, bio-sensing etc. The surface affinity is governed by both enthalpic (relative interactions between the species and surface) and entropic (excluded volume) effects. Neglecting enthalpic effects i.e. for purely athermal systems, entropy is the only driving force that controls the surface affinity of the species in a binary or multi-component mixture. Many intensive (relative size of colloids, chain length, equilibrium bond angle, chain flexibility) and extensive (confinement, temperature) factors can dramatically change the entropy of the system and thus enhance or decrease the surface affinities of the constituent species. In this article, we use coarse grained metropolis Monte Carlo simulations to delineate the role of these factors on entropic surface segregation in binary mixture of polymers and colloids. At low number densities, excluded volume effects are negligible and we do not observe any entropic driven surface segregation. Therefore our system of interest is binary polymer-colloids mixtures at moderate to high number densities where excluded volume effects are predominant. Our results indicate that for flexible polymer chains, the surface is always enriched with colloids compared to polymers and this effect is enhanced for longer polymer chains. The configurational entropy of the flexible polymers is significantly reduced near the surface and therefore they prefer to stay in bulk (away from the surface). However this behavior can be completely reversed by introducing large degree of confinement and making the chains relatively rigid (less flexible). Our results show that polymer segregation of long stiff chains in slit pore geometry is driven by nematization near the surface while looping of polymers is observed under large degree of confinement. We observe that for longer polymer chains with an equilibrium bond angle (q = p), both confinement and chain stiffness enhance the surface segregation of polymers relative to colloids.However, the segregation behavior within a confinement is dependent on the polymer chain length. The surface segregation of polymers is dramatically decreased for chains with equilibrium bond angles; pi/3, pi/2, 2pi/3 and 5pi/6 independent of chain length and flexibility due to excluded volume effects as this leads to inefficient packing near the surface.

title: Applying Computer Science to the Development of Chemical Reactions: Applications in Heck-Type Cross-Coupling Reactions
abstract: Organic chemistry and computer science have historically been immiscible. My research is focused on harnessing the power of computer science to streamline the development of chemical reactions, in particular using high throughput experimentation (HTE) to study Heck-type coupling reactions. These reactions require a metal center supported by a ligand, and reactivity and selectivity are dictated by the multifaceted interactions of the pairing. These reactions often produce mixtures of nearly identical products, commonly including enantiomers whose separation and classification prove uniquely challenging. Through the design of a novel program and user interface, we are able to parse large data sets of yield and selectivity - particularly those generated by HTE - and present the information in a meaningful way. Graphical representations, partially analyzed with MATLAB and Python and coupled with intuition and prior experience, aid chemists in rapid interpretation of these data sets. Challenges emerged in the design of the program: representations need to be generated quickly, be meaningful at a glance, and be created by users unaccustomed to data science. These considerations are being addressed in the design process.

title: Quantifying United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Using Greenscope Indicators
abstract: The 2015 United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals were created with ambition to construct a better world by the year 2030. These goals suggest how we should live, and how companies should conduct their businesses. However, they are quite broad with limited ways of quantification. This work proposes a framework that could be used to quantify such goals so that systems’ evolutions can be evaluated at different times in their operating cycles. Using the chemical process sustainability assessment tool GREENSCOPE, sets of indicators that represent specific UN Sustainable Development Goals are identified and used to quantify a given target within a goal. The identified indicators may be grouped in categories: resource efficiency, recycling, waste management, and resilience. After choosing a set of GREENSCOPE indicators, a case study of an Acetic Acid manufacturing simulation in CHEMCAD is analyzed. Sections of the manufacturing process are studied and discussed to determine their performance in terms of resilience and sustainability.

title: Evaluation of Solvent Recovery Options for Economic Feasibility through a Superstructure-Based Framework
abstract: As the chemical market continues to expand, the concerns with regards to environmental sustainability have increased due to excessive disposal of chemical solvents. To date, there is no proper mitigation plan to handle such volume of chemical waste. Solvents are used in many industries for purposes such as reaction medium and as extraction, cleaning, and purification agents. These solvents can account for up to 90% of the process by mass and are often discarded after a single use. Incineration, the most widely used process for solvent disposal, is not a “green” method due to the potential detrimental effects to the environment. A systematic framework for solvent recovery has been developed which considers multiple alternative recovery and purification technologies to recover solvents simultaneously through a superstructure-based approach. These technologies are represented as mathematical models that are composed of material and energy balances, utility requirements, equipment design, and costs to assist in determining the most economical method for solvent recovery of any chemical waste stream. Two case studies involving simple binary solvent system and a more complex multi-component system were analyzed and formulated as mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. Selecting solvent recovery options required considerably lower cost in comparison to typical incineration. The solutions obtained from the case studies presented in this work demonstrated the capability of the solvent recovery framework to obtain environmentally friendly and economically viable solvent recovery pathways as an alternative to incineration.

title: Rapid Assessment of Chemical Toxicity Using Machine Learning and Combinatorial Quantitative-Structural Analysis Relationship Models
abstract: Due to the nature of their work, United States Airmen and other members of the armed services can be exposed to harmful chemicals that may degrade their physical and/or cognitive performance. Additionally, on-the-ground personnel may require rapid assessment of a chemical’s toxicity; laboratory testing is often too slow to provide an adequate response. Therefore, there is a real need for rapid, robust, and accurate in-silico models that can computationally predict key toxicological activities. Quantitative structural-activity relationship models, or QSAR, are becoming popular as models of choice with the rise of machine learning in the field. The developed Python QSAR package, named as QSARBayesOpt, employs combinatorial QSAR, an emerging type of model in the cheminformatics community. Using consensus voting, the predicted values from each independent model are combined to increase the predictive power of the package as a whole. Through this automatic tuning framework, the package allows the end-user to easily change datasets using Bayesian optimization. Bayesian optimization is also an intelligent tuning method, learning from previous iterations to make smarter searches in the parameter space; therefore, significant amount of computational time and cost can be saved using this approach. Furthermore, we have tested this package against several datasets, including inhibition activity of acetylcholinesterase by organophosphates, where we saw 78% regression accuracy and 97% classification accuracy.

title: Mathematical Modeling of the Influence of Toxin Exposure on Rheumatoid Arthritis
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis is a debilitating autoimmune disease that attacks the joints in the body. These attacks cause chronic inflammation that degrades the surrounding bone overtime. This disease effects around one percent of the population globally, and women are three times more likely to be diagnosed with this disease than men. Rheumatoid arthritis research is broad with many scientific studies underway to identify causes, cures, and preventions. Previous studies have determined the mechanism of the disease once it becomes established in the body, but only limited published results focus on identifying triggers and mapping the physiological responses at the onset of arthritis. It is understood that environmental factors account for seventy percent of the disease generation, while genetics accounts for the other thirty percent. Recent studies have shown that the immune responses to environmental factors that lead to arthritis may begin in the gut, gums, or lungs years before symptoms appear. However, the links between the timing and extent of various environmental exposures on the onset and progression of arthritis are not clearly understood. Mathematical models can provide insights into explaining the complex linkages between molecular level actions of chemicals and their effects on the cellular, tissue, and whole body levels of physiology in a disease. We are building a model for the chemical and biological processes that are theorized to be involved in the onset of arthritis. To model how environmental toxins, such as herbicides and bacteria, stimulate chronic inflammation, we have combined two previously published models into a more complex and informative model. This model tracks how the concentration of tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a chemical that triggers inflammation, changes in the joints, the bloodstream, and the surrounding tissue. The model predicts TNF regulation by the inflammatory stress on the immune system. We will explore possible explanations for how specific toxins can alter TNF regulation to lead to arthritis. This work will impact society by improving fundamental understanding of the effects of toxins on arthritic autoimmune inflammation, laying the scientific foundation for advances in disease treatment and prevention.

title: Performing Quantum Chemical Computations at Different Levels of Theory to Predict Am(III) over Eu(III) Selectivity for DTPA-Based Ligands
abstract: The presence of minor actinides (especially Americium) in spent nuclear fuel has posed a veritable challenge for the long-term storage of nuclear waste due to their high radiotoxicity and thermal emission. Minor actinides also have the potential to be reused in nuclear fuel cycle, making it further desirable for their extraction. However, despite the development of polyaminocarboxylate ligands that can achieve the problematic separation of Am(III) from trivalent lanthanides via selective complexation of the former, insufficient theoretical understanding of the molecular chemistry behind such complexation has hindered the design of more efficient and industrially attractive ligands. These theoretical obstacles arise primarily from challenges in computationally describing (1) heavy metal electronic structures and (2) the increase in covalent interactions between polyaminocarboxylate ligands and Am(III) compared to Ln(III). This work aims to determine a reliable computational protocol in predicting the Am(III) over Eu(III) selectivity of a polyaminocarboxylate ligand by evaluating the performance of ab initio quantum chemistry computations at various levels of theory, including density functional theory, Post-Hartree-Fock, and multiconfigurational methods. We also employed basis sets of varying degrees of flexibility for light and heavy atoms each. In our search for a protocol that provides reasonable accuracy while expending as few resources as possible, our results have potentially shown not only the importance not only of utilizing basis sets of sufficient size, but also of examining how a particular computational method accounts for electron correlation and relativistic effects. Further evaluation of these computational methods to other similar systems as well as comparing their results with experiment are needed in order to systematically corroborate their predictive ability.

title: Application of Machine Learning Methods to Improve Leukemia Diagnostics
abstract: In 2019, there will be an estimated 1,762,450 new cancer cases diagnosed and 606,880 cancer deaths in the United States [1] . With both numbers increasing every year it is very important to be able to diagnose each and every patient in the most cost efficient and timely manner. Every patient that is suspicious of having any type of cancer will undergo multiple tests to find a correct diagnosis. It has become extremely important to assess the signs of cancer in patients with the most accurate test possible for efficient diagnosis. Biomarkers, external symptoms, and other important indicators allow medical professionals to evaluate the cancer status upon examination. One of the most prominent markers that appear within the blast cells of patients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is myeloperoxidase (MPO) [2] . This project has focused on the use of machine learning methods to evaluate the chances of a patient having AML or Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) based on the clinical variables obtained via morphological, and cytochemistry tests. The two machine learning methods used in this study were decision trees and neural networks. These methods require a data set to train the neural network or decision tree and then a testing data set to evaluate how accurately these machine learning methods identify each patient as having ALL or AML. The immunophenotyping (IPT) results serve as the confirmatory test for checking the solution accuracy. These machine learning approaches can possibly help to determine which symptoms/markers are most important to search for when diagnosing a patient with either AML or ALL. A marker is deemed to be significant when it is used as a node within the tree and as for the neural network there are weights assigned to each possible marker with the more important markers resulting in a higher weight. It will also help to inform doctors which tests will be most efficient in determining a diagnosis for patients. It was found that the decision tree approach was able to diagnose patients with AML 97.14% of the time when considering myeloperoxidase (MPO). The neural network that was created using the same dataset was able to classify patients correctly 100% of the time while assigning the highest weight to the MPO marker. To check for the significance of the MPO marker both the decision tree and neural network were recreated neglecting the MPO marker. Both machine learning methods had a drop in accuracy when classifying a patient with AML with the accuracy of decision trees falling to 91.43% and the neural networks decreasing to 90.91%.

title: The Interaction of Azole Bio-Isosteres with Amino Acid Side Chains for Drug Design
abstract: There is significant interest in the design of new drugs with novel binding sites for interactions with specific peptides in proteins. The hydrogen bond is a key noncovalent interaction governing what happens between a drug molecule and its local environment. For drug molecules, this local environment can be a biological target, a biological off-target, aqueous solution, a lipid membrane, or even a crystalline solid. Consequently, hydrogen bonding impacts a wide range of molecular properties critical to drug design including potency, selectivity, membrane permeability, and solubility. This project is investigating the energetics of hydrogen bonding at the fundamental level to gain new insights into the basicity of a molecular site and its role in controlling hydrogen bond interactions as well as the possibility of proton transfer from one site to another. We are using the amide group as a model for the protein backbone as it can work both as a hydrogen donor and acceptor. At this point, there is no single model that explains the large range of binding energies exhibited by such hydrogen bonds. We are modeling the interactions of the basic amino acids, lysine, arginine and histidine with the non-classical amide bio-isosteres 3,5 dimethyl-1,2,4-triazole and 2,5-dimethyl-2H-tetrazole using computational electronic structure methods at the ab initio correlated molecular orbital theory and density functional theory levels. The structures are initially optimized using density functional theory to probe different conformations and binding sites. This information is used as input into more computationally demanding correlated molecular orbital theory calculations at the G3(MP2) level to predict the energetic properties of these azoles and their hydrogen bonding interactions with different amino acid side chains. Besides the gas phase calculations, the basicities and hydrogen bond energies in different solutions are predicted using self-consistent reaction field approaches to provide better insights into what is happening in a biochemical environment.

title: Analysis and Simulation of FCC Unit Using Aspen HYSYS
abstract: In the preliminary step of petroleum refinery, crude oil is processed and fractionated into lighter hydrocarbons which have lower ignition point i.e., petroleum naphtha, gasoline or diesel. Inherently, product stream of fractional distillation column other than the lighter hydrocarbons also contain heavier hydrocarbons which is often referred to as residue (gasoil). Due to the higher ignition point, it is deemed to be less economically valuable product. To serve this purpose, Fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) is employed to add more value to the heavier products. FCC is one of the most important processes in the petroleum refining industry for the conversion of heavy gasoil that provides about 35% to 45% of the blending stocks in refinery of gasoline. Various alkenes like ethylene and propylene are also produced by FCC for polymer applications. This work describes the model of FCC in ASPEN HYSYS that can simulate the behavior of FCC close to real work conditions. The FCC models mainly consists of riser, stripper, reactor and regenerator. In this work, a basic refinery process is designed and the vacuum gas oil from the vacuum distillation column is used as feed in the FCC unit. A sensitivity analysis is carried on parameters of interest i.e., pressure difference between regenerator and reactor, catalyst heat capacity, feed temperature , to determine the correlation that affect the FCC performance (mole-fraction of Butane is used to measure the performance) . The typical data in refinery is adopted, in which few changes were made in order to achieve proper simulation. The results of simulation predict the parameters which are more sensitive towards the performance of FCC, for example, performance of FCC is more sensitive to change in heat capacity of catalyst as compared to feed temperature. Hence, with this model, set of parameters are determined which have pre-dominant effect to FCC’s performance.

title: Mathematical Modeling of Mesangial Cells in Diabetic Kidney Disease
abstract: Diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease. About one out of four adults with diabetes has kidney disease. The kidney is supposed to filter wastes and extra water out of the blood stream to produce urine. When the kidney is damaged, it cannot filter blood like it should, which leads to waste build up and excess water in the body and eventually to death. One of the key cell types damaged in the kidney is mesangial cells. The mesangial cells and the surrounding extracellular matrix hold together the bundles of capillaries where blood is filtered in the kidneys. Experiments have shown multiple chemical pathways that change mesangial cells in diabetic kidney disease (DKD). It is challenging to describe how these chemical pathways interact with each other in mesangial cells over time. I have used mathematical modeling of differential equations to represent the chemical pathways in mesangial cells that are known to be affected by DKD. I have combined the separate pathways into a systems biology model that can consider the interactions between pathways and between multiple mesangial cells in the kidney. I will present model results for conditions that lead to expansion of the mesangial tissue (cells and extracellular proteins) during diabetic hyperglycemia.

title: Computer Modeling of Aerosol Diffusion through Lung Mucosa
abstract: Diseases of the lung are some of the most common and deadly in the world. Existing treatments, if any exist, tend to be extremely invasive and time-consuming. Further, due to the poor bioavailability of drugs traditionally administered orally or through injection, these treatments are not very effective. Technology is emerging that allows an aerosolized drug dosage to be delivered directly to the diseased area; however, the mucus layer separating the airways from the tissue remains a barrier to this method. The mucociliary clearance mechanism in the lungs clears foreign particles (including cigarette ash, dust, and bacteria) and prevents infection. A layer of mucus on the surface of the inner lung is constantly pushed upward towards the throat by a bed of cilia, and most particles that impact on the mucus are cleared from the lungs quickly and without incident. Although mucociliary clearance aims to prevent a disease from being contracted, it remains a barrier to drug delivery, as drugs must cross the same thick mucus layer that is being swept away from the tissue. We used COMSOL Multiphysics software to develop a model of the mucosal interface between the airways and the lung tissues. Data from the literature is used to determine details like dimensions, velocity, and viscosity. The mucus layer moves upwards towards the throat in laminar flow, imitating the mucociliary effect, and the underlying periciliary layer has no net movement due to the regular beating of the cilia that move the mucus. The “drug” enters from the airway side and moves through the fluid by convection. Given these inputs, the model outputs the concentration distribution of the administered drug molecule or particle subject to diffusion through the moving mucosa. We aim to maximize the amount of drug that reaches the target lung tissue. The model is customizable, easily modified to simulate other drugs or any other particle so long as some properties are known. Variables have been specifically parametrized to find more complex relationships, like effective diffusivity, from an input of more readily available information, like particle radius. Lung conditions can also be altered to meet the needs of the application (for example, the mucus layer is much thinner in the alveolar region, and the mucus of cystic fibrosis patients is much denser than average). Thus, the model can provide insight into the efficacy of new lung treatments and aid in the design of drug transport properties.

title: Simulation and Optimization of Epoxypropane Preparation Process Via Hppo Based on Aspen Plus
abstract: A continuous HPPO lab-scale pilot plant was designed for the production of propene oxide via HPPO (Hydrogen Peroxide Propene Oxide) process. It is necessary to optimize the technical parameters for improving epoxypropane yield. In this paper, Aspen Plus software was introduced to simulate the main units of Hydrogen Peroxide Propene Oxide, such as Epoxidation Reaction unit, Propylene Circulation unit, Epoxypropane Purification unit and Propylene glycol Purification unit. In the reaction, propylene is epoxidized with H 2 O 2 over a TS-1 catalyst using methanol/water as a solvent. The reaction occurs at a temperature and pressure of 52℃ and 3 MPa, respectively. HAZOP and P&ID were conducted for the reactor and distillation column. Aspen Sensitivity was employed to proceed the sensitivity analysis of dividing wall column (DWC), double effect distillation column, extract distillation column and azeotropic distillation column. The optimized key technical parameters were obtained by Aspen simulation. The main objective of the simulation is to complete the design and optimization of a plant that produces 337,000 metric tonnes per year (8000hr) of propylene oxide (PO) and 21,000 metric tonnes per year (8000hr) of propylene glycol (PG). Through simulation, the mass fraction of propylene oxide in the product is greater than 99.3%, and the mass fraction of by-product propylene glycol is greater than 99.99%. The model can be considered of high utility in designing and optimizing HPPO process, to achieve high reactants conversion and propene oxide yields.

title: Mathematical Modeling of Nephrin Loss in Diabetic Kidney Disease
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of kidney failure. The job of the kidneys is to filter the blood. However, when the kidneys are damaged, the filtration system is less efficient. In this project we focused on podocyte cells, which compose the outer filtration barrier. In between podocyte cells, a protein called nephrin connects the podocytes like Velcro. The blood is filtered through this area to excrete waste and excess water. Diabetes can cause the nephrin to lose its Velcro abilities causing it to disconnect from the podocyte cells and be excreted in the urine. The loss of nephrin causes the mountain and valley landscape of the podocytes and the gaps between them to become distorted. Diabetic complications can cause the nephrin to lose the Velcro ability and be excreted. We will present an empirical model for predicting category of proteinuria (protein in the urine) based on loss on nephrin expression using human biopsy data for Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes patients. Type 1 and Type 2 have different blood sugar landscapes, this potentially causes differences in nephrin loss. We will also present images from a graphical user interface that we developed, with graphs presenting nephrin expression in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes. The model relates the percentage of nephrin lost to the mRNA expression of nephrin and to the urinary protein concentration. This noninvasive modeling research provides quantitative guidance for the threshold where nephrin loss causes long-term damage to the kidney clinically detectable by the presence of protein in the urine.

title: Computational Screening of Environmental Barrier Coating Materials for Nuclear Thermal Propulsion Engines
abstract: Although nuclear thermal propulsion (NTP) rocket engines have the potential to far outperform the state-of-the-art chemical combustion engines for interplanetary travel, corrosive interactions between the hydrogen propellant and the uranium fuel element acts as a serious barrier of entry for the application of NTP engines. Environmental Barrier Coatings (EBC) have been considered previously to protect the elements but coating techniques used did not enough control to be effective. This research investigated the use of Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) as a technique to coat fuel spheres with a nanoscale EBC to prevent hydrogen attack on the fuel. ALD allows a conformal, uniform, and nanometer thick coating on both the fuel spheres as well as the high aspect ratio channels of the fuel elements. The primary focus of this study was the coating material to be deposited via ALD. Potential candidates were selected based on low neutron cross sections and high melting points. Density functional theory (DFT), a computational quantum mechanical modelling method, was then employed to calculate energy barriers for a hydrogen atom to move through both the surface unit cells and the bulk unit cells of these candidate materials. Those with the highest barriers were deposited on surrogate materials and compared to materials previously investigated for this application. Samples were characterized to ensure deposition was successful and determine film thickness. Stability of materials in a high hydrogen environment was also studied with DFT. This predicted stability was then tested experimentally in a high temperature furnace system. Through this process, it was shown that nitrides are predicted to outperform pure metals when used as EBCs in NTP engines and many will remain stable at very high temperatures. It was also demonstrated that both tungsten nitride (WN) and molybdenum nitride (MoN) are not stable enough species for this application. Candidate materials from this work will be deposited on surrogate substrates to be experimentally compared to each other, as well as barrier materials previously investigated for this application, in future work.

title: Binding of Lignin Dimers on MWW-2D Zeolite: Solvothermal Effect Study
abstract: Lignin as the potential renewable source of biofuels, chemicals, and other value-added products has gained significant attention. However, due to its complex structural network, developing efficient depolymerization techniques are challenging. Lignin depolymerization is governed by reaction conditions (pressure, temperature, etc.), catalyst used, and the presence of solvent. In this work, the binding modes of different β-O-4 linkages have been analyzed using periodic density functional theory (DFT) with the optB88-vdW functional. The effect of how changing the ratio of H to OH on the catalytic surface, different temperatures, and different solvents affects the binding energy has been analyzed. Overall, model MWW framework zeolites are characterized by ab-initio first principle simulations, with the goal of gaining molecular level insights into the different binding modes of β-O-4 linkages on the catalytic surface.

title: Electronic Properties of Dicationic Ionic Liquids for Corrosion Inhibition
abstract: Ionic liquids have been found to impart corrosion inhibition performance in industrial applications. In order to assess the corrosion potential of several imidazolium-based dicationic ionic liquids, quantum mechanical calculations were performed to predict their electronic properties. The structure of these dicationic ionic liquids was R 1 -Im-R 2 -Im-R 3 where R 1 , R 2 , R 3 are alkyl chains and Im are imidazolium rings. Three alkyl chain lengths (butyl, hexyl, and octyl) were studied for R 1 and R 3 , whereas ethyl, butyl, and hexyl groups were considered for the linker domain R 2 for a total of 15 cations. These cations were paired with two chloride Cl - , two tetrafluoroborate [BF 4 ] - and an equimolar mixture of Cl - -[BF 4 ] - resulting into a total of 51 cation-anion pairs. Population analysis was carried to obtain electrostatic potential maps and HOMO-LUMO energy gaps. The HOMO-LUMO gap and optimized structures were analyzed to discern patterns in their gas phase behavior based on length of alkyl chains and the configuration of anions. The HOMO-LUMO energy gap was found to be the most dependent on the anion, with pure Cl - exhibiting the lowest gap, while the pure [BF 4 ] - showing the highest when comparing structures with equivalent cations. The most important factor found to affect the structure of the studied ionic liquids was the length of the alkyl chain linking the two imidazolium moieties. From the structural respective, Cl - location in the optimized geometry was decided by the acidic hydrogen atoms on the imidazolium rings due to its tendency to hydrogen bond. [BF 4 ] - also participated in the hydrogen bonding, but increased area of negative charge in the anion allowed it to bridge the imidazolium rings more effectively. A novel behavior was found when the [BF 4 ] - anion was present along with the butyl group as the linker in which the cation curled up on itself, creating a large region of positive charge within the center of the molecule.

title: Theoretical Design and Analysis of High-Spin Ground-State a-D-a-π Conjugated Polymers
abstract: Theoretical design and analysis of high-spin ground-state A-D-A-π conjugated polymers John D. Teas , Md Abdus Sabuj and Neeraj Rai Dave C. Swalm School of Chemical Engineering and Center for Advanced Vehicular Systems, Mississippi State University, MS, 39762, USA. High-spin ground-state donor-acceptor (DA) conjugated polymers (CPs) used as organic semiconductors (OSCs) are prevalent in research spanning the fields of physics, chemistry, and materials science. The OSCs with open-shell character have applications in many modern technologies, including organic electronics, nonlinear optics, and energy conversion and storage. Alternating arrangement of DA CPs exhibit various properties, such as interactions with light, the ability to transport charges, and tunability through chemical modification, which also allow for the active usage of these OSCs in optoelectronic technology (London et al , 2019). However, due to the presence of unpaired electrons, these high-spin organic molecules are unstable and highly localized. Despite these challenges, computer simulation allows for the design and analysis of these high-spin organic materials. Here, we have designed three conjugated A-D-A-π polymer semiconductor structures that show signs of having a triplet ground state ( S = 1) in the long polymer chain limit. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations at the unrestricted (U)B3LYP/6-31G** level of theory were performed on the oligomers ( n = 1 to 5) to identify the evolution of their electronic properties. The diradical character index (0 < y < 1), which describes the contribution of the open-shell resonance form to the ground-state, was found to be y = 0.537 for n = 1 and y = 0.999 for n = 5. This implies the formation of a pure diradical ( y = 1) for longer polymer chain lengths. The singlet-triplet energy gap (ΔE ST ) decreases with an increase in the length of the polymer chain ( ΔE ST = 0.114 eV for n = 1 and ΔE ST = 2.7x10 -6 eV for n = 5), which shows the extent of electron exchange interactions from admixing of the HOMO and LUMO in the ground state. This study shows the possibility to synthesize new A-D-A-π polymers, which are stable at ambient conditions, with intriguing molecular and electronic properties.

title: Analytical Prediction of Non-Newtonian Concentration Profiles Using a Correction Factor
abstract: Mathematical models are a vital part of chemical engineering. Modelling systems allows for predictions to be made in specific cases without a dependence on empirical data alone. In fluid mechanics, models of systems containing Newtonian fluids can be easily obtained by established methods. However, Non-Newtonian fluids are much more difficult to model. The introduction of a correction factor could allow for Newtonian models to be used for Non-Newtonian fluids. Due to the nature of dimensionless or reduced states, the non-dimensionalized models for two different fluids under the same conditions are equivalent. By non-dimensionalizing a Newtonian model and then applying a correction factor, the characteristics of the model could be adjusted to match the hypothetical non-Newtonian case. With this method, the documented solution for a system containing a Newtonian fluid could be used to generate a model of the same system with a non-Newtonian fluid. The use of a correction factor to obtain a model of a non-Newtonian system significantly reduces the amount of time and computational power that would typically be required for such a task. This contribution proposes a method to obtain velocity and concentration profiles of a system containing a non-Newtonian fluid through the use of a correction factor and the analytical solution to the same system with a Newtonian fluid. The proposed analytical solution will be compared to the numerical solution to prove the accuracy of this method.

title: Computational Analysis of C-H Hydroxylation in Bio-Inspired Monometallic Complexes
abstract: With sustainable energy innovations on the rise but logistical and technological barriers preventing their widespread implementation, it is of paramount importance to increase the sustainability of conventional energy generation for the remainder of its lifecycle. Natural gas, despite being the most environmentally benign of the fossil fuels, is underutilized due to difficulties in storage and transportation. Catalytic C-H hydroxylation is achieved in nature by enzymes known as lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) . The goals of this research project are twofold: To quantify the difference in energy barriers faced by a singlet and triplet state catalytic complex To determine whether a one step or two step reaction mechanism is energetically favorable for this C-H hydroxylation process Computational methods are applied to bio-inspired catalytic systems, utilizing quantum mechanical algorithms to optimize initial and final molecular geometries and determine stable transition state structures. The relevant energy and entropy differences are then calculated and compared between the spin states and pathways, shedding further light on the nuanced and controversial mechanisms by which these biological complexes catalyze C-H hydroxylation, and potentially enabling more effective catalyst design. Tentative preliminary results are consistent with literature values.

title: Generalized Antoine and Wagner Equations Consistent with the Predictions of the Soave-Redlich-Kwong Equation of State Using Similarity Variables
abstract: Chemical engineers use the Wagner and Antoine equations to correlate vapor pressure as a function of temperature for various substances; however, they do not describe the entire vapor pressure curve from the triple point to the critical point. Methods of finding generalized Antoine and Wagner equation constants consistent with the predictions of the Soave-Redlich-Kwong (SRK) equation of state were studied. Calculations were simplified using two similarity variables. Common adjusted temperature, η * , combined reduced temperature and acentric factor, and common adjusted pressure, ψ*, combined reduced pressure and reduced temperature. Results of an iterative SRK vapor pressure algorithm were transformed into a data set of the new similarity variables. Antoine and Wagner constants were empirically determined by nonlinear least squares to achieve less than 0.05 percent relative deviation from SRK predictions. Three common adjusted temperature subranges, from the critical point down to 0.23, were needed for the Wagner equation. Only the C constant was fitted by least squares for the Antoine equation, with the A and B constants determined by exact calculation at the endpoints of common adjusted temperature ranges. Five common adjusted temperature subranges, from the critical point down to 0.18, were needed for the Antoine equation.

title: Volume Change of Vaporization from the SRK Equation of State Using a Similarity Variable
abstract: Equations of state such as the Soave-Redlich-Kwong (SRK) equation are used to predict thermodynamic properties of chemical substances. Most commonly, PVT properties are directly calculated, but equilibrium properties such as volume change of vaporization may be calculated using more complex algorithms including fugacity calculations. In this project, direct calculation methods for estimating volume change of vaporization consistent with the SRK equation were studied. Reduced volume change of vaporization, ΔV R , was expressed as a power series of natural adjusted temperature η, a similarity variable combining reduced temperature and acentric factor. Starting from a previously determined reduced density power series, twenty series coefficients were derived. Series results were compared to exact SRK data for volume change of vaporization, and the relative deviation was less than 0.22 percent for natural adjusted temperatures between 0.0516 and the critical point. Work continues to find additional series coefficients and increase the range of natural adjusted temperatures while keeping the relative deviation within 0.5 percent, and to combine the reduced volume change of vaporization series with the Clapeyron equation to calculate heat of vaporization.
